summary.text: A 54-year-old current smoker without major previous illness developed dysarthria, nystagmus and severe ataxia at 09:30. He arrived alert and afebrile with NIHSS 4, BP 165/90 mmHg, heart rate 103/min and oxygen saturation 98% on room air; acute CT/CTA and routine screening did not explain the presentation.

Suspected vertebrobasilar stroke prompted 73 mg IV alteplase at 13:40 without improvement. At 17:00 he deteriorated with somnolence, agitation, hyperventilation and severe metabolic acidosis despite no hemorrhage on repeat CT. Ventilation and bicarbonate were required; his wife reported recent depression and suicidal thoughts. Empiric 10 g of 10% ethanol was started, toxicology confirmed ethylene glycol 95.85 mg/dL, and ICU hemodialysis followed.

Renal function worsened within 48 hours with urine calcium oxalate crystals; fever and radiographic pneumonia prompted IV antibiotics. CT at 24 hours remained normal. Ethylene glycol cleared and pH normalized by day two, permitting dialysis cessation. He was extubated on day five and disclosed approximately 0.5–1 dL antifreeze ingestion with suicidal intent before arrival; psychiatric transfer occurred day nine, followed by symptom-free discharge.

All first and 48-hour table measurements remain separately indexed. Admission headings for initial ABG/toxicology conflict with narrative sampling after deterioration, so they do not establish an initial severe-acidosis encounter.

summary.text: A 78-year-old man with hypertension, diabetes and Parkinson disease developed noon-onset vertigo, gait impairment and dysarthria. At 15:00 he was alert and oriented with nystagmus, gaze palsy, limb/truncal ataxia and NIHSS 5; vital signs, initial imaging and screening laboratory results were unremarkable. He denied alcohol or sedative use.

Thrombolysis at an onset-to-needle interval of 194 minutes did not improve symptoms. At 21:00 coma, tetraplegia, Babinski signs and absent brainstem reflexes required ventilation; CT/CTA again excluded hemorrhage or large-vessel occlusion. Severe acidosis with pH below 6.8, lactate above 15 mmol/L and ethylene glycol 159 mg/dL prompted circulatory support, ICU ethanol/CRRT, bicarbonate and vitamins.

Ethanol was stopped after pH normalized and ethylene glycol remained below 20 mg/dL, but anuria, worsening creatinine to 6.2 mg/dL and oxalate crystalluria persisted. Day-five pneumonia required broad-spectrum antibiotics; he remained comatose despite stopping sedation and died on day ten. Later depressed mood and an empty antifreeze bottle were reported, but intent was not established.
Serial first, nine-hour and 48-hour measurements are distinct. The first ABG/toxicology table admission label conflicts with the later narrative workup; exact sample timing is unresolved.

summary.text: A 54-year-old man with hypertension, chronic alcohol-related illness and a prior right-hemispheric stroke with residual left spastic hemiparesis/Babinski sign had a brief loss of consciousness at 13:30. Severe aphasia, confusion and agitation followed (NIHSS 7); seizure was suspected but no convulsion signs were detected. IV clonazepam and tiapride treated agitation. Imaging showed only chronic infarction and no acute hemorrhage or arterial occlusion; sodium was 122 mmol/L.

IV rt-PA 0.9 mg/kg at 17:20 did not change neurological status. Toxicology was negative for ethanol but positive for ethylene glycol at 16.54 mg/dL; the narrative describes physiological acid-base parameters. ICU ethanol was given, renal function remained stable and dialysis was not indicated.

Ethylene glycol was undetectable the next day. Aphasia/agitation diminished while hyponatremia, attributed provisionally to chronic alcoholism, was corrected slowly with saline. By day three he walked with minor assistance and managed self-care; he denied intentional antifreeze use. He went home on day six with his previous residual neurological deficits, rather than a fully normal neurological examination.

First and 48-hour laboratory values are retained separately, including source calcium 0.24 mmol/L without correction. Initial ABG/toxicology admission labels do not settle their collection times relative to thrombolysis.
